The paper analyzes the integration applicability of active infrared (IR) stealth technology under radar stealth design constraints.
The simulation compares the thermal response and infrared contrast characteristics of radar-absorbing materials (RAM) and metal surfaces.
RAM has a lower thermal conductivity (0.5 W/m·K) and higher heat capacity (1,200 J/kg·K) compared to aluminum (205 W/m·K, 900 J/kg·K).
RAM forms a distinct high-temperature region at the center of the surface, leading to high temperature gradients and increased infrared contrast.
Metal surfaces maintain a more uniform temperature distribution, resulting in lower infrared contrast against the background.
RAM takes approximately 3.5 seconds to reach a stable average surface temperature of 39.25°C, while metal reaches 34°C in just 1.5 seconds.
RAM exhibits a higher standard deviation of 3.47°C in surface temperature, compared to 0.88°C for metal.
The infrared simulations show a wider distribution of pixel brightness for the RAM surface, indicating higher infrared contrast.

The paper proposes three design strategies for integrating IR and RF stealth technologies: local thermal control, multilayer structures with high thermal conductivity, and optimization of thermal inertia distribution.
These strategies aim to mitigate the structural constraints between RAM-based RF stealth and IR stealth requirements.
The study provides a technical foundation for designing integrated IR-RF stealth systems and enabling the development of more versatile, multifunctional stealth platforms.
The study is based on simulation results and does not include validation with real-world experiments.
Future research could focus on integrating the simulation findings with experimental data and exploring the performance under various operational scenarios.
The paper highlights the inherent conflicts between the thermal properties required for RF and IR stealth technologies.
Addressing these conflicts is crucial for the development of effective multispectral stealth capabilities.
